## Learning goals

Chapters 11 to 13 assumed that the central bank sets the interest rate at which firms and households borrow. In a
financial crisis that link breaks. This chapter adds a **risk premium** to the short-run model and uses it, together
with U.S. data, to study the financial crisis of 2008–2009, the dangers of deflation and the policy response. By the
end of it you will be able to:

- add the **financial friction** $\bar{f}$ to the IS/MP model, derive the **new AD curve** step by step, and show why
  the friction acts like a negative demand shock;
- solve the AS/AD model period by period for output and inflation, derive the long run and the speed of adjustment,
  and read the **comparative statics** of a higher risk premium;
- derive the best output the Fed can reach at the **zero lower bound**, and show with the Fisher equation why a
  **deflationary spiral** can turn a recession into a depression;
- use balance-sheet algebra (leverage, capital requirements), present values and the term structure to explain the
  policy responses: bank rescues, quantitative easing, forward guidance and fiscal stimulus;
- read the data on the crisis and its aftermath (interest-rate spreads, the Taylor rule, potential GDP, money growth,
  asset-price bubbles, the Fed's balance sheet, forward guidance and productivity), and compare the U.S. experience
  with dozens of other economies;
- in Python: build a model step by step from small functions, compute peaks, troughs and growth rates, stack a
  chart with `px.area`, rebuild a table from monthly data, blank out data that cross a definition break, and pick
  countries from a list (`SelectMultiple`) with a color that stays fixed for each country.

<!-- cell -->

## Model overview

**Islandia** has had a good run, until a housing boom on the island turns to bust and fear spreads through its banks. Lenders now ask Harbor Boatworks and the islanders for a much higher rate than before, even though the Bank of Islandia is cutting its own rate as fast as it can. Prices start to fall, and the central bank soon has no room left to cut. Can a scare in the banks drag a whole island into a deep slump, and what can policy do about it? This section adds the missing link, a **risk premium**, to the short-run model of Chapters 11 to 13 and follows Islandia through the crisis.

::: {.callout-note .mo-bigidea title="The big idea"}
**The question.** Why can a financial crisis cause a deep recession even when the central bank cuts its interest rate all the way to zero?

**The answer in one sentence.** Firms and households borrow at the central bank's rate *plus* a premium, so a jump in that **financial friction** hits spending exactly like a fall in demand, and at the **zero lower bound** falling prices push the real rate up and can start a **deflationary spiral**.

**What goes in and what comes out.** We choose the demand shock, the risk premium, the inflation target, how hard the central bank reacts, the slope of the Phillips curve and, for the policy block, the balance-sheet and asset-price numbers. The model gives back output, inflation and interest rates year by year, the best output the central bank can reach at the zero bound, and how much a bank or a share loses in a crash.

**Road map.**

1. [The IS/MP model with a financial friction](#the-ismp-model-with-a-financial-friction): the [assumptions](#assumptions), [solving the model](#solving-the-model) step by step, and [what the model predicts](#what-the-model-predicts).
2. [The new AD curve](#the-new-ad-curve-a-financial-friction-in-the-asad-model): the friction in the AS/AD model, [solved period by period](#solving-the-model-1), with its [long run and comparative statics](#what-the-model-predicts-1).
3. [Deflation and the zero lower bound](#deflation-and-the-zero-lower-bound): the Fisher equation, the floor on the real rate and the [deflationary spiral](#solving-the-model-2).
4. [Balance sheets, leverage and the policy responses](#balance-sheets-leverage-and-the-policy-responses): the [definitions](#definitions), the algebra of leverage, asset prices, quantitative easing, forward guidance and fiscal stimulus, and [a table of the policies](#what-the-model-predicts-3).
5. [Model in code](#model-in-code): the key results as Python functions, checked with numbers, followed by the [drawing tools](#drawing-and-data-tools) for the diagrams and the [tools for the data figures](#drawing-and-data-tools) (recession shading and a peak-to-trough calculator).

**Notation.** A bar over a letter marks a **parameter**, a number set outside the model; letters without a bar are **endogenous variables** that the model solves for. Short-run output $\tilde{Y}_t$ is the percentage gap between actual and potential output, and all interest and inflation rates are in percent per year. In the code we write `a`, `f`, `m`, `B_BAR`, `NU`, and so on.

| Symbol | Meaning | Type |
|---|---|---|
| $\tilde{Y}_t$ | short-run output: the percent gap between actual and potential output | endogenous |
| $R_t$ | the real rate that firms and households pay on their loans | endogenous |
| $R^{ff}_t$ | the real fed funds rate: the central bank's own policy rate | endogenous |
| $\pi_t$, $\pi^e_t$ | inflation, and the inflation people expect | endogenous |
| $i_t$, $i^{ff}_t$, $i^L_t$ | nominal rates: the borrowing rate, the fed funds rate, an $n$-year rate | endogenous |
| $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, $\bar{r}$ | the demand shock, the interest sensitivity of demand, the marginal product of capital | parameters |
| $\bar{f}$ | the risk premium (the financial friction) | parameter |
| $\bar{\pi}$, $\bar{m}$, $\bar{x}$ | the inflation target, the response to inflation, the response to output | parameters |
| $\bar{\nu}$ | the slope of the Phillips curve | parameter |
| $\bar{i}$ | a nominal rate that is stuck (at the bound, or by choice) | parameter |
| $\pi_C$, $\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t$ | long-run inflation; the best output reachable at the zero lower bound | endogenous |
| $\lambda$, $\kappa$ | leverage and the capital ratio of a balance sheet | endogenous |
| $P$, $E$, $g$ | an asset's price, next year's profits, and their growth rate | notation |
| $R^{ff,*}$, $x_t$ | the rate that restores potential output; inflation's distance from $\pi_C$ | notation |
:::

### The IS/MP model with a financial friction

#### Assumptions

**Islandia in numbers.** The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers, apart from a few examples. Here the algebra, the checks and every diagram of the notebook share one illustrative baseline:

- the IS curve: a marginal product of capital $\bar{r} = 2$ percent and $\bar{b} = 1$, so each point of interest rate above $\bar{r}$ costs 1 percent of output;
- the policy rule and the Phillips curve: an inflation target $\bar{\pi} = 2$ percent, $\bar{m} = 1$ and $\bar{\nu} = 0.5$;
- the 2008 scenario: a housing bust lowers demand by $\bar{a}' = -2$, and the panic adds a risk premium $\bar{f} = 4$ points;
- the 1929 scenario: the central bank raises its rate by 3 points, and a stock market crash lowers demand by $\bar{a}' = -3$.

The two scenarios are named after the U.S. episodes that the figures study. With these values the model gives the textbook's example numbers: $-2$ and $-4$ percent in Fig. 2, and $-3$, $-6$ and $-9$ percent in Figs. 12 and 13.

**1. The IS curve** (Chapter 11). Harbor Boatworks invests less, and islanders spend less, when the real rate $R_t$ they pay climbs above the marginal product of capital $\bar{r}$. Short-run output follows:

$$\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).$$

The demand shock $\bar{a}$ gathers every reason to spend more or less at a given interest rate: confidence, household wealth, government purchases, exports. The parameter $\bar{b} > 0$ says how strongly investment responds to the rate.

**2. The central bank sets the fed funds rate.** The Bank of Islandia controls the (real) **fed funds rate** $R^{ff}_t$, the overnight rate at which Islandia's banks lend to one another. (We keep the U.S. name, since the data come from there.) Chapters 11 to 13 treated this as the rate that firms pay. From now on it is not.

**3. The financial friction.** Islandia's banks add a premium $\bar{f} \geq 0$ on top of the fed funds rate when they lend to firms and households. It pays them for the chance that a loan goes bad:

$$R_t = R^{ff}_t + \bar{f}. \tag{1}$$

In quiet years $\bar{f}$ is near zero, and the central bank in effect sets the borrowing rate itself. In a panic $\bar{f}$ shoots up. Fig. 1 measures it in the data as the gap between the yields on corporate and government bonds.

<!-- cell -->

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the IS curve in terms of the Fed's rate.** Replace $R_t$ in the IS curve by equation (1), then pull $\bar{f}$ out of the bracket:

$$\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t + \bar{f} - \bar{r}) = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}).$$

The first two terms do not depend on the central bank, so they form one combined demand shock, $\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}$.

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words"}
Harbor Boatworks does not ask why its loan got dearer. Whether the central bank raised its rate or the banks raised their premium, the boatyard pays more and builds fewer boats. So, seen from the rate the Bank of Islandia controls, a bigger premium looks just like a drop in demand.
:::

**Step 2: the rate that restores potential output.** Suppose the central bank wants $\tilde{Y}_t = 0$. Set the left side to zero, move $\bar{b}(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r})$ across and divide by $\bar{b}$ ([Appendix C.9](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.9-solving-equations-and-systems)):

$$0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R^{ff}_t - \bar{r} = \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}} - \bar{f}.$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the IS curve with a financial friction"}
$$\tilde{Y}_t = \underbrace{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}_{\text{demand shock}} - \bar{b}\,(R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}) \tag{2}$$

$$R^{ff,*} = \bar{r} + \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}} - \bar{f} \tag{3}$$

Equation (2) is the IS curve drawn against the rate the central bank sets. Equation (3) says that the bank must offset the demand shock (the term $\bar{a}/\bar{b}$) *and* cut one extra point for each point of premium.

**Islandia in numbers.** In the 2008 scenario, $\bar{a}' = -2$ and $\bar{f} = 4$, so (3) asks for $R^{ff,*} = 2 - 2 - 4 = -4$ percent.
:::

**Step 3: the 2008 example in numbers.** With $\bar{a}' = -2$ and $\bar{b} = 1$, the crisis comes in three stages:

- *the housing bust, and the central bank does nothing* ($R^{ff} = \bar{r} = 2$, $\bar{f} = 0$): $\tilde{Y} = -2 - 0 = -2$ percent (point $B$ of Fig. 2);
- *the bank cuts to the rate (3) with $\bar{f} = 0$*: $R^{ff} = 2 + (-2)/1 = 0$ percent and $\tilde{Y} = 0$ (point $C$);
- *the panic adds $\bar{f} = 4$, but the bank stays at 0*: Harbor Boatworks pays $R = 0 + 4 = 4$ percent, and $\tilde{Y} = -2 - 1\times(4 - 2) = -4$ percent (point $D$).

Getting output back to potential would take a fed funds rate of $-4$ percent. The third block explains why the central bank cannot go that low.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
The rate that matters for spending is the central bank's rate plus the risk premium, so a panic acts like a demand shock.
:::

<!-- cell -->

#### What the model predicts

**Comparative statics.** Equation (2) is a straight line, so each effect is a fixed number: the derivative of $\tilde{Y}_t$ with respect to that parameter ([Appendix C.7](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.7-derivatives-and-marginal-thinking)).

| A one-point rise in ... | changes $\tilde{Y}_t$ by | What moves in the IS/MP diagram | What the central bank must do, from (3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| the risk premium $\bar{f}$ | $-\bar{b} = -1$ point | the MP line (the rate firms pay) shifts **up** by 1 | cut $R^{ff}$ by 1 point |
| the fed funds rate $R^{ff}$ | $-\bar{b} = -1$ point | the MP line shifts up by 1 | (this *is* the bank's tool) |
| the demand shock $\bar{a}$ | $+1$ point | the IS curve shifts **right** by 1 | raise $R^{ff}$ by $1/\bar{b} = 1$ point |

- **A friction is a demand shock.** At a fixed policy rate, one more point of $\bar{f}$ costs $\bar{b}$ points of output, the same as a fall of $\bar{a}$ by $\bar{b}$.
- **The central bank can undo it, point for point,** as long as it is free to cut $R^{ff}$ far enough. With $\bar{f} = 2$ in our example, the premium cancels the bank's cut of 2 points, and $D$ falls on top of $B$.
- **Two shocks add up.** Against the bank's starting rate, the bust and the premium together cost $\bar{a}' - \bar{b}\bar{f}$. Once the cut has offset the bust, what remains is $-\bar{b}\bar{f} = -4$ percent.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Each point of premium needs one extra point of rate cuts, which is easy in normal times and impossible near zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** A milder panic hits Islandia: the housing bust is still $\bar{a}' = -2$, but the premium is only $\bar{f} = 2$. The central bank has cut its rate to 0 percent. What is short-run output, and what fed funds rate would close the gap?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By the IS curve with equation (1), firms pay $R = 0 + 2 = 2$ percent, so $\tilde{Y} = -2 - 1\times(2 - 2) = -2$ percent: the premium has undone the whole cut. Equation (3) asks for $R^{ff,*} = 2 - 2 - 2 = -2$ percent.

</details>

**2.** On the IS/MP diagram, does a higher premium shift the IS curve or the MP line?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The MP line, if we plot the rate that firms pay: equation (1) lifts it by $\bar{f}$ at any fed funds rate. Plotted against the fed funds rate instead, equation (2) shows the same event as a shift of the IS curve to the left by $\bar{b}\bar{f}$. Both views give the same output.

</details>
:::

<!-- cell -->

### The new AD curve: a financial friction in the AS/AD model

#### Assumptions

Keep the IS curve and equation (1). Add the other two pieces of the AS/AD model of Chapter 13:

**4. A monetary policy rule.** The Bank of Islandia moves its rate with the gap between inflation and its target,

$$R^{ff}_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}), \qquad \bar{m} > 0.$$

**5. The AS curve.** The Phillips curve with adaptive expectations ($\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}$): inflation climbs above last year's rate when output is above potential,

$$\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.$$

Each year the model solves for four unknowns, $\tilde{Y}_t$, $\pi_t$, $R^{ff}_t$ and $R_t$. Last year's inflation $\pi_{t-1}$ is already known.

<!-- cell -->

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the borrowing rate under the rule.** Put the rule into equation (1). Take $\bar{r}$ away from both sides of (1) first:

$$R_t - \bar{r} = (R^{ff}_t - \bar{r}) + \bar{f} = \bar{f} + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).$$

Whatever rate the rule sets, Islandia's banks add the premium on top.

**Step 2: the new AD curve.** Put this into the IS curve and group the terms that do not depend on inflation:

$$\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\left[\bar{f} + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\right].$$

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the new AD curve"}
$$\tilde{Y}_t = \underbrace{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}_{\text{AD shock}} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{4}$$

It is the AD curve of Chapter 13 with $\bar{a}$ replaced by $\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}$. It slopes down: higher inflation makes the central bank raise its rate, and output falls.
:::

To draw it with inflation on the vertical axis, solve (4) for $\pi_t$:

$$\pi_t = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \tilde{Y}_t}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.$$

**Step 3: this period's output and inflation.** Islandia sits where AD and AS cross. Replace $\pi_t$ in (4) by the AS curve $\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t$:

$$\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.$$

Gather the $\tilde{Y}_t$ terms on the left, $(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\,\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})$, and divide:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: output and inflation each year"}
$$\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}, \qquad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t \tag{5}$$

Given last year's inflation, the first formula gives this year's output, and the AS curve then gives this year's inflation.

**Islandia in numbers.** With $\bar{b} = \bar{m} = 1$ and $\bar{\nu} = 0.5$ the denominator is $1.5$. In the first year of the 2008 scenario $\pi_{t-1} = \bar{\pi} = 2$, so $\tilde{Y}_1 = (-2 - 4 - 0)/1.5 = -4$ percent and $\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5\times(-4) = 0$ percent: point $B$ of Fig. 3.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words: the rule as a shock absorber"}
The AD shock is $-6$, yet output falls by only 4 percent in the first year. The reason is the rule. As the slump pulls inflation down, the Bank of Islandia cuts its rate, and that cut softens the blow to Harbor Boatworks. Without any response, the whole shock of 6 points would land on output.
:::

**Step 4: the long run.** If the shocks persist, Islandia settles where inflation stops changing. By the AS curve, $\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}$ only when $\tilde{Y}_t = 0$. Set $\tilde{Y} = 0$ in (4) and solve for inflation:

$$0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_C - \bar{\pi}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_C - \bar{\pi} = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.$$

**Step 5: how fast the economy gets there.** Measure inflation by its distance from the long run, $x_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_C$. Step 4 says $\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} = \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_C - \bar{\pi})$. Use this in the numerator of (5):

$$\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_C - \bar{\pi}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_C) = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,x_{t-1},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \tilde{Y}_t = \frac{-\bar{b}\bar{m}\,x_{t-1}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.$$

Next, subtract $\pi_C$ from both sides of the AS curve and insert this expression for $\tilde{Y}_t$:

$$x_t = x_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = x_{t-1}\left(1 - \frac{\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\right) = \frac{x_{t-1}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.$$

Repeat this step $t$ times ([Appendix C.10](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.10-difference-equations-how-macro-variables-move-over-time)) to reach the result below.

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the long run and the speed of adjustment"}
$$\pi_C = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}} \tag{6}$$

$$\pi_t - \pi_C = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\right)^{t}(\pi_0 - \pi_C) \tag{7}$$

Output goes back to potential, but inflation ends at $\pi_C$, and each year the remaining gap shrinks by the same factor.

**Islandia in numbers.** $\pi_C = 2 + (-6)/1 = -4$ percent: output recovers at point $C$, but with **deflation**. With a factor of $1/1.5$, one third of the gap closes each year. From $\pi_0 - \pi_C = 6$, inflation goes to $\pi_1 = 0$ and then $\pi_2 = -4 + 6\times\tfrac{4}{9} \approx -1.3$ percent, on its way to $-4$.
:::

By the formula for $\tilde{Y}_t$ in Step 5, output runs $-4$, then $-2.7$, then $-1.8$ percent. Inflation keeps falling until the rule has cut the borrowing rate far enough to offset both shocks.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Under a policy rule the slump fades year by year, but inflation ends lower, possibly below zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** Suppose the Bank of Islandia reacts twice as hard, $\bar{m} = 2$, in the 2008 scenario. What is output in the first year, and what share of the remaining inflation gap closes each year?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Now $1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1 + 1\times2\times0.5 = 2$. By equation (5), $\tilde{Y}_1 = -6/2 = -3$ percent instead of $-4$. By equation (7) the gap is multiplied by $1/2$ each year, so half of it closes every year, faster than the one third of the baseline.

</details>
:::

<!-- cell -->

#### What the model predicts

**Comparative statics.** Each effect follows from equations (5) and (6) by differentiating with respect to one parameter. The numbers use our baseline, $1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1.5$.

| A one-point rise in ... | AD curve | output in the first year | inflation in the first year | long-run inflation $\pi_C$ | long-run output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the demand shock $\bar{a}$ | shifts right by 1 | $+\frac{1}{1.5} = +0.67$ | $+\frac{\bar{\nu}}{1.5} = +0.33$ | $+\frac{1}{\bar{b}\bar{m}} = +1$ | 0 |
| the risk premium $\bar{f}$ | shifts left by $\bar{b} = 1$ | $-\frac{\bar{b}}{1.5} = -0.67$ | $-0.33$ | $-\frac{1}{\bar{m}} = -1$ | 0 |

- **The friction is an AD shock.** A higher $\bar{f}$ moves the AD curve toward lower output at every inflation rate, just as a lower $\bar{a}$ would. The AS curve stays put at first. That is Fig. 3.
- **The recession passes; the lower inflation stays.** Output returns to potential, but inflation settles $1/\bar{m}$ lower for each point of premium. Starting from just 2 percent, a big enough shock ends in deflation: $\pi_C < 0$ whenever $\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} < -\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\pi}$, here whenever the AD shock is worse than $-2$.
- **A tougher rule helps.** A larger $\bar{m}$ flattens AD. The first-year recession $(\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f})/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})$ gets smaller, $\pi_C$ falls by less, and by (7) the economy converges faster.
- **The hidden assumption.** The rule must always be able to deliver the real rate it calls for. The next block shows how deflation and the zero lower bound break this, which is why the textbook turns to the IS/MP diagram for such times (Figs. 12 and 13).

::: {.mo-takeaway}
A risk premium shifts AD left: a temporary recession, but a permanent fall in inflation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** A milder panic: $\bar{a}' = -2$ and $\bar{f} = 2$, starting from $\pi_0 = 2$. What are output and inflation in the first year, and where does inflation end up?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The AD shock is $-2 - 2 = -4$. By equation (5), $\tilde{Y}_1 = -4/1.5 \approx -2.7$ percent and $\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5\times(-2.67) \approx 0.7$ percent. By equation (6), $\pi_C = 2 + (-4)/1 = -2$ percent: even this milder panic ends in deflation.

</details>

**2.** Does the risk premium lower Islandia's output in the long run?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. By the AS curve, inflation keeps falling as long as output is below potential, and every fall makes the rule cut the rate. The economy only comes to rest at $\tilde{Y} = 0$. The premium shows up in the long run as lower inflation, $1/\bar{m}$ per point by equation (6), not as lower output.

</details>
:::

<!-- cell -->

### Deflation and the zero lower bound

#### Assumptions

**6. The Fisher equation** (Chapter 12). The nominal interest rate $i_t$ is the real rate plus inflation, $i_t = R_t + \pi_t$. Take $\pi_t$ from both sides to get the real rate, the one in the IS curve:

$$R_t = i_t - \pi_t. \tag{8}$$

(The textbook prints this rearranged equation with a plus sign in place of the minus. That is a typo: the surrounding text uses the minus.) The same link holds for the central bank's rate: the nominal fed funds rate is $i^{ff}_t = R^{ff}_t + \pi_t$.

**7. The zero lower bound.** A nominal rate cannot go (much) below zero, $i^{ff}_t \geq 0$. Islanders can always keep cash under the mattress, and cash earns exactly zero, so nobody would lend at less.

<!-- cell -->

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the nominal rate a rule asks for.** Add $\pi_t$ to both sides of the policy rule, and let the rate react to output as well (the **Taylor rule** of Chapter 13, with weight $\bar{x}$ on output):

$$i^{ff}_t = R^{ff}_t + \pi_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t. \tag{9}$$

Taylor's original values, $\bar{r} = \bar{\pi} = 2$ and $\bar{m} = \bar{x} = 0.5$, give $i^{ff}_t = 2 + \pi_t + 0.5\pi_t - 1 + 0.5\tilde{Y}_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t + 0.5\,\tilde{Y}_t$, the rule drawn in Fig. 4. In our AS/AD baseline ($\bar{m} = 1$, $\bar{x} = 0$) it reads $i^{ff}_t = 2 + \pi_t + (\pi_t - 2) = 2\pi_t$. So the rule wants a negative nominal rate as soon as inflation turns negative, which on the path of equation (7) happens from period 2 on. Fig. 3 silently assumes a cut that the Bank of Islandia could not make.

**Step 2: the floor on the real rate.** Put $i^{ff}_t \geq 0$ into $R^{ff}_t = i^{ff}_t - \pi_t$: the real fed funds rate can go no lower than $-\pi_t$. By equation (1), the lowest rate Harbor Boatworks can pay is then $\bar{f} - \pi_t$.

**Step 3: the best output the central bank can reach.** Put this lowest borrowing rate into the IS curve:

$$\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(\bar{f} - \pi_t - \bar{r}).$$

Multiply out the bracket and collect the terms in $\bar{r}$ and $\pi_t$:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the best output at the zero lower bound"}
$$\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f} + \bar{b}\,(\bar{r} + \pi_t) \tag{10}$$

The bound **binds** when the rate the bank needs, (3), lies below the floor, $R^{ff,*} < -\pi_t$, which is the same as $\tilde{Y}^{\max}_t < 0$.

**Islandia in numbers** (2008 scenario, $\bar{a}' = -2$, $\bar{f} = 4$). With inflation at 2 percent, $\tilde{Y}^{\max} = -2 - 4 + 1\times(2 + 2) = -2$ percent, so even a zero nominal rate only gets output back to $B$. With zero inflation the best is $-4$ percent, and with 2 percent deflation it is $-6$ percent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words"}
At the bound, inflation becomes the Bank of Islandia's last lever on the real rate. While prices rise, a zero nominal rate still means a negative real rate, which helps Harbor Boatworks. Once prices fall, the same zero nominal rate means a *positive* real rate, and the best the bank can do gets worse with every point of deflation.
:::

**Step 4: the deflationary spiral.** Now let the nominal rate be stuck at some $\bar{i}$, either at the bound or because the central bank will not move it (as the Fed did in the early 1930s). Borrowers judge the real rate by the inflation they expect, which under adaptive expectations is last year's: $R_t = \bar{i} - \pi_{t-1} + \bar{f}$. The IS curve turns into

$$\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(\bar{i} + \bar{f} - \bar{r}) + \bar{b}\,\pi_{t-1}.$$

Write the same equation for the year before and subtract it. All the terms with a bar drop out:

$$\tilde{Y}_t - \tilde{Y}_{t-1} = \bar{b}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-2}) = \bar{b}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_{t-1},$$

where the last step uses the AS curve one year back, $\pi_{t-1} - \pi_{t-2} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_{t-1}$. Add $\tilde{Y}_{t-1}$ to both sides:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the deflationary spiral"}
$$\tilde{Y}_t = (1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu})\,\tilde{Y}_{t-1} \tag{11}$$

With the nominal rate frozen, each year's output gap is a fixed multiple, larger than one, of last year's.

**Islandia in numbers.** $1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu} = 1.5$, so a gap of $-6$ percent becomes $-9$, then $-13.5$ percent: the slump deepens by 50 percent each year.
:::

This is the step from $C$ to $D$ in Figs. 12 and 13 (the 1929 scenario). The crash leaves output at $-6$ percent with inflation at zero. The slump then drags inflation to $0 + 0.5\times(-6) = -3$ percent, the real rate rises by 3 points, and output sinks to $-9$ percent.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
At the zero lower bound falling prices raise the real rate, and a slump can feed on itself.
:::

<!-- cell -->

#### What the model predicts

- **Deflation raises the real rate.** By (8), with $i_t$ fixed, each point less of inflation adds a point to the real rate. In normal times the central bank just cuts $i_t$; at the zero lower bound it has no room.
- **Comparative statics at the bound**, from equation (10): $\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\pi = +\bar{b}$ (each point of deflation costs $\bar{b} = 1$ point of reachable output), $\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\bar{f} = -\bar{b}$, and $\partial\tilde{Y}^{\max}/\partial\bar{a} = +1$. In the IS/MP diagram, deflation and a higher premium both push the lowest possible MP line up.
- **Stable versus unstable.** Put equations (7) and (11) side by side. Under a rule with $\bar{m} > 0$, falling inflation *lowers* the real rate, and the gap shrinks by the factor $1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) < 1$ each year. With the nominal rate frozen, falling inflation *raises* the real rate, and the gap *grows* by the factor $1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu} > 1$. The only resting point is $\tilde{Y} = 0$, and the economy drifts away from it: a **deflationary spiral**. In the terms of equation (4), a frozen nominal rate works like a rule with a *negative* $\bar{m}$.
- **Ways out.** Anything that raises $\tilde{Y}^{\max}$ in (10) helps:
  - a higher $\bar{a}$ (fiscal stimulus by the Islandia Treasury);
  - a lower $\bar{f}$ (rescuing the banks);
  - higher expected inflation (anchored expectations, money growth);
  - lower *long-term* rates through asset purchases and forward guidance.

  The next block puts numbers on these. **Secular stagnation** is the case in which $R^{ff,*}$ in (3) stays below the floor for years.

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** In the 2008 scenario ($\bar{a}' = -2$, $\bar{f} = 4$), Islandia's inflation has slipped to 1 percent and the nominal rate is at zero. What is the best output the central bank can reach?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (10), $\tilde{Y}^{\max} = -2 - 4 + 1\times(2 + 1) = -3$ percent. The bound binds: even at a zero rate, output stays 3 percent below potential.

</details>

**2.** Islandia's nominal rate is frozen, and output is 4 percent below potential this year. What does the model predict for next year, and why does the slump get worse?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (11), next year's gap is $1.5\times(-4) = -6$ percent. The slump lowers inflation by $\bar{\nu}\times4 = 2$ points. With the nominal rate stuck, the Fisher equation (8) turns that into a real rate 2 points higher, which costs $\bar{b}\times2 = 2$ more points of output.

</details>
:::

<!-- cell -->

### Balance sheets, leverage and the policy responses

#### Definitions

**Balance sheet.** For one of Islandia's banks, a household or the central bank, what it owns equals what it owes plus what is left over for its owners:

$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Net worth}.$$

**Leverage** (Chapter 10) is the ratio of liabilities to net worth, $\lambda \equiv \text{Liabilities}/\text{Net worth}$. A **capital requirement** sets a minimum for the **capital ratio** $\kappa \equiv \text{Net worth}/\text{Assets}$.

**Present value.** An asset that pays profits $E$ next year, growing at the rate $g$ every year after that, is worth the sum of those profits discounted at the interest rate $R > g$ ([Appendix C.12](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.12-present-value-and-discounting)).

**The term structure** (Chapter 12). An $n$-year interest rate is roughly the average of the short rates expected over the next $n$ years.

<!-- cell -->

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: leverage and the capital ratio.** Divide the balance sheet by net worth: $\text{Assets}/\text{Net worth} = \lambda + 1$. The capital ratio $\kappa$ is the inverse of that ratio, so

$$\kappa = \frac{1}{1 + \lambda} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda = \frac{1 - \kappa}{\kappa}.$$

A capital requirement is therefore a cap on leverage. A 7 percent requirement permits $\lambda = 0.93/0.07 \approx 13.3$; a 20 percent requirement permits only $\lambda = 4$.

**Step 2: why leverage magnifies losses.** A bank's debts are fixed in money terms. If its assets lose the share $x$ of their value, the entire loss, $x\cdot\text{Assets}$, falls on net worth. As a share of net worth:

$$\frac{\Delta\,\text{Net worth}}{\text{Net worth}} = -\,x\,\frac{\text{Assets}}{\text{Net worth}}.$$

Since $\text{Assets}/\text{Net worth} = 1 + \lambda = 1/\kappa$:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: leverage magnifies losses"}
$$\frac{\Delta\,\text{Net worth}}{\text{Net worth}} = -(1 + \lambda)\,x = -\frac{x}{\kappa} \tag{12}$$

**Islandia in numbers.** A bank with a 7 percent capital ratio loses $3/0.07 \approx 43$ percent of its net worth when its assets lose 3 percent. It is **insolvent** (net worth below zero) once they lose more than $\kappa = 7$ percent. A 20 percent ratio absorbs a 20 percent fall.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .mo-inwords title="In words"}
Think of an Islandia bank's capital as a cushion between its assets and its depositors. Leverage measures how thin that cushion is. A small fall in house prices goes straight through a thin cushion, which is why lenders panic and raise $\bar{f}$. When the Islandia Treasury injects capital into a bank (as TARP did in the United States), it thickens the cushion and lowers $\lambda$.
:::

**Step 3: asset prices.** The present value of the growing stream of profits is a geometric series with ratio $q = (1+g)/(1+R) < 1$:

$$P = \frac{E}{1+R} + \frac{E(1+g)}{(1+R)^2} + \frac{E(1+g)^2}{(1+R)^3} + \dots = \frac{E}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - q} = \frac{E}{1+R}\cdot\frac{1+R}{R - g}.$$

Divide both sides by $E$:

::: {.callout-important .mo-key title="Key result: the price-earnings ratio"}
$$\frac{P}{E} = \frac{1}{R - g} \tag{13}$$

**Islandia in numbers.** If shares in Harbor Boatworks are priced with $R = 7$ percent and $g = 2$ percent, $P/E = 1/0.05 = 20$. One more point on the discount rate, say from a higher risk premium, gives $1/0.06 \approx 16.7$: share prices drop by about 17 percent.
:::

Take logs ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)): $\ln P = \ln E - \ln(R - g)$, so $d\ln P/dR = -1/(R - g) = -20$. A rise in $R$ of 0.01 (one point) lowers $\ln P$ by about 0.2. That is the slope at the baseline; over a whole point the exact fall is the 17 percent above, because the slope flattens as $R - g$ widens. A ratio far above anything plausible values of $R - g$ can justify signals a **bubble** (Figs. 7 and 8). When such prices collapse, islanders' wealth shrinks and $\bar{a}$ falls.

**Step 4: the Fed's balance sheet.** For the central bank the identity is

$$\text{Treasuries} + \text{MBS} + \text{other assets} = \text{Currency} + \text{Reserves} + \text{other liabilities}.$$

**Quantitative easing** buys assets other than short-term government bonds, such as mortgage-backed securities (MBS) or long-term Treasuries. The central bank pays by crediting reserves to the sellers' banks, so both sides grow by the same amount and no new currency is printed. Table 14.1 (in the *Key numbers* of Fig. 9) checks this identity in the U.S. data.

**Step 5: forward guidance.** Write the $n$-year rate as the average of the expected short rates,

$$i^{L}_t \approx \frac{i_t + i^e_{t+1} + \dots + i^e_{t+n-1}}{n}. \tag{14}$$

Even with today's rate $i_t$ stuck at zero, the central bank can push the long rate down by promising to keep *future* rates low. Take a 4-year bond. If markets expect short rates of 0, 1, 2 and 3 percent, the long rate is $6/4 = 1.5$ percent. A believable promise of zero for three years (0, 0, 0, 2) brings it down to $2/4 = 0.5$ percent. Fig. 10 shows such a shift in market expectations.

**Step 6: fiscal stimulus at the bound.** Government purchases are part of $\bar{a}$. At the zero lower bound the interest rate does not rise when $\bar{a}$ goes up, so by equation (10) a stimulus lifts reachable output one for one: closing the gap takes $\Delta\bar{a} = -\tilde{Y}^{\max}$. In the 2008 scenario that is 2 percent of potential output with inflation at 2 percent, but 6 percent once 2 percent deflation has set in. Delay makes the job bigger.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
Thin capital cushions turn small price falls into bank failures, and a panic about them is what lifts the risk premium.
:::

<!-- cell -->

#### What the model predicts

| Policy | Which term it moves | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| cut the fed funds rate | $R^{ff}$ in (2) | works until the floor $-\pi$ of (10) |
| rescue banks (TARP), higher capital ratios | $\bar{f}$ in (1), $\lambda$ in (12) | lower premium; smaller losses in the next crisis |
| quantitative easing | long-term and mortgage rates, (13) and (14) | lower borrowing rates beyond the fed funds rate |
| forward guidance | expected future rates in (14) | lower long rates at a zero short rate |
| fiscal stimulus | $\bar{a}$ in (2) and (10) | raises output one for one at the bound |
| anchored inflation expectations | $\pi$ in (10), the spiral (11) | keeps the real rate from rising |

- **Leverage turns small price falls into crises.** By (12), a fall in asset prices of a few percent can wipe out a highly leveraged bank. The fear of such losses is what raises $\bar{f}$.
- **Higher capital requirements** shrink $1 + \lambda$ in (12). They are the most direct way to make the next crisis smaller.
- **Asset prices react strongly to the discount rate** when $R - g$ is small, by (13). Booms and busts in share and home prices move islanders' wealth, and so $\bar{a}$.

::: {.mo-takeaway}
When the policy rate is stuck at zero, policy works on the other terms: the premium, long rates, expectations and spending.
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-check title="Check your understanding"}
**1.** An Islandia bank holds a capital ratio of 10 percent. What is its leverage, and how much of its net worth does it lose if its assets fall by 4 percent?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By Step 1, $\lambda = (1 - 0.1)/0.1 = 9$. By equation (12), net worth falls by $4/0.1 = 40$ percent. A fall of more than 10 percent in its assets would leave the bank insolvent.

</details>

**2.** The Bank of Islandia's rate is at zero and markets expect short rates of 0, 2 and 4 percent over the next three years. What is the 3-year rate, and what does it become if the bank credibly promises 0, 0 and 1 percent?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

By equation (14), the 3-year rate is $(0 + 2 + 4)/3 = 2$ percent before the promise and $(0 + 0 + 1)/3 \approx 0.33$ percent after it. Forward guidance lowers long-term borrowing costs for Harbor Boatworks without any change in today's rate.

</details>
:::

::: {.callout-note .mo-recap title="Recap"}
- **The risk premium** $\bar{f}$ separates the rate firms pay from the central bank's rate, $R_t = R^{ff}_t + \bar{f}$, and jumps in a panic (measured by the bond spread of Fig. 1).
- **A friction is a demand shock:** in the IS curve (2) and the new AD curve (4) it enters as $\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{f}$, so the central bank must cut one extra point per point of premium ([Fig. 2](#fig.-2-a-housing-bubble-and-a-financial-crisis)).
- **Under a policy rule** the recession fades at the rate of equation (7), but inflation settles at $\pi_C$ from (6), which can be below zero ([Fig. 3](#fig.-3-the-financial-crisis-in-the-asad-framework)).
- **At the zero lower bound** the best reachable output (10) falls with every point of deflation, and with a frozen nominal rate the gap grows by $1 + \bar{b}\bar{\nu}$ a year, a deflationary spiral (11) ([Fig. 12](#fig.-12-the-great-depression-in-the-ismp-framework), [Fig. 13](#fig.-13-the-phillips-curve-and-the-great-depression)).
- **Leverage and asset prices:** a bank loses $x/\kappa$ of its net worth when its assets lose $x$, and $P/E = 1/(R - g)$ makes prices very sensitive to the discount rate (the bubbles of Figs. 7 and 8).
- **Policy beyond the policy rate:** bank rescues, quantitative easing, forward guidance (14) and fiscal stimulus each raise $\tilde{Y}^{\max}$ ([Fig. 9](#fig.-9-financial-assets-of-the-federal-reserve), [Fig. 10](#fig.-10-the-fed-funds-rate-actual-and-expected)).
:::

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next
helper builds those versions. Run it and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. one of the IS/MP diagrams
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "f"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

### The model as functions

The model has four blocks: the IS curve with a financial friction, the new AD curve, the zero lower bound and
the balance sheets. We write each Key result as a Python *function*: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives
back a result. The first cell sets Islandia's baseline values, the constants that every function and figure
uses, and then writes the IS/MP block: the IS curve (2), the borrowing rate (1) and the Fisher equation (8).

```{python}
# Islandia's baseline. Names in capital letters, such as `R_BAR`, are constants:
# we set them once and never change them.
# Step 1: the IS curve: marginal product of capital r-bar = 2%,
# interest sensitivity b = 1
R_BAR, B_BAR = 2.0, 1.0
# the policy rule and the AS curve: inflation target 2%, policy response m = 1,
# Phillips slope nu = 0.5
PI_BAR, M_BAR, NU = 2.0, 1.0, 0.5
# 2008: the housing bust a' = -2 and a risk premium f = 4 points
A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS = -2.0, 4.0
# 1929: the Fed's hike of 3 points and the crash a' = -3
HIKE, A_CRASH = 3.0, -3.0


# Step 2: the IS/MP block, one function per equation.
# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# `a=0.0` gives a a default value, used whenever we do not pass one.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def is_output(R, a=0.0):
    """Short-run output on the IS curve, in percent.

    The IS curve:  Y~ = a - b (R - r-bar). With R = R_ff + f from equation (1),
    this is equation (2).

    Arguments
        R : the real interest rate that firms and households pay, in percent
        a : the demand shock, a-bar (0 unless we pass another value)
    Returns
        short-run output, Y~, in percent
    """
    # `return` gives back the result
    return a - B_BAR * (R - R_BAR)


def is_rate(Y, a=0.0):
    """The IS curve solved for the real interest rate (used to draw the curve).

    Equation (2) solved for R:  R = r-bar + (a - Y~) / b

    Arguments
        Y : short-run output, Y~, in percent
        a : the demand shock, a-bar
    Returns
        the real interest rate R, in percent
    """
    # the same line as is_output, read from Y~ to R
    return R_BAR + (a - Y) / B_BAR


def borrowing_rate(R_ff, f=0.0):
    """The rate at which firms and households borrow.

    Equation (1):  R = R_ff + f

    Arguments
        R_ff : the (real) fed funds rate, in percent
        f    : the risk premium, f-bar, in percentage points
    Returns
        the borrowing rate R, in percent
    """
    # the banks add the premium on top of the central bank's rate
    return R_ff + f


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """The real interest rate, from the Fisher equation.

    Equation (8):  R = i - pi

    Arguments
        i  : the nominal interest rate, in percent
        pi : inflation, in percent
    Returns
        the real interest rate R, in percent
    """
    # the nominal rate minus what inflation takes away
    return i - pi
```

The AS/AD block needs three more functions: the new AD curve (4), the AS curve and the point where the two cross,
equation (5).

```{python}
def ad_output(pi, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Short-run output on the new AD curve.

    Equation (4):  Y~ = (a - b f) - b m (pi - pi-bar)

    Arguments
        pi : inflation, in percent
        a  : the demand shock, a-bar
        f  : the risk premium, f-bar
        m  : how hard the central bank reacts to inflation, m-bar
    Returns
        short-run output, Y~, in percent
    """
    # the friction enters exactly like a fall in demand, a - b f
    return a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi - PI_BAR)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_prev=PI_BAR):
    """Inflation on the AS curve (the Phillips curve).

    The AS curve, the second half of equation (5):  pi = pi_prev + nu Y~

    Arguments
        Y       : short-run output, Y~, in percent
        pi_prev : last period's inflation, in percent
    Returns
        this period's inflation, pi, in percent
    """
    # a boom (Y~ > 0) pushes inflation above last year's
    return pi_prev + NU * Y


def solve_asad(pi_prev, a=0.0, f=0.0, m=M_BAR):
    """This period's output and inflation, where the AD and AS curves cross.

    Equation (5):  Y~ = (a - b f - b m (pi_prev - pi-bar)) / (1 + b m nu),
                   pi = pi_prev + nu Y~

    Arguments
        pi_prev : last period's inflation, in percent
        a       : the demand shock, a-bar
        f       : the risk premium, f-bar
        m       : how hard the central bank reacts to inflation, m-bar
    Returns
        two numbers: short-run output Y~ and inflation pi, both in percent
    """
    # Step 1: output from the first half of equation (5)
    Y = (a - B_BAR * f - B_BAR * m * (pi_prev - PI_BAR)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * NU)
    # Step 2: inflation from the AS curve; a comma returns both numbers at once
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_prev)
```

The last cell holds three small functions for the zero lower bound and for balance sheets: the best output at the
bound (10), the loss of net worth (12) and the price-earnings ratio (13).

```{python}
def zlb_best_output(pi, a=0.0, f=0.0):
    """The highest output the central bank can reach with its nominal rate at zero.

    Equation (10):  Y~max = a - b f + b (r-bar + pi)

    Arguments
        pi : inflation, in percent
        a  : the demand shock, a-bar
        f  : the risk premium, f-bar
    Returns
        the best reachable short-run output, Y~max, in percent
    """
    # with i = 0 the real rate is -pi, so deflation (pi < 0) lowers the ceiling
    return a - B_BAR * f + B_BAR * (R_BAR + pi)


def net_worth_change(asset_fall, capital_ratio):
    """The percent change in a bank's net worth when its assets lose value.

    Equation (12):  change in net worth / net worth = -x / kappa

    Arguments
        asset_fall    : the fall in the value of the assets, x, in percent
        capital_ratio : net worth over assets, kappa (e.g. 0.07)
    Returns
        the change in net worth, in percent
    """
    # leverage magnifies the loss: a 7% capital ratio turns 1% into about 14%
    return -asset_fall / capital_ratio


def price_earnings(R, g):
    """The price-earnings ratio of a share.

    Equation (13):  P/E = 1 / (R - g)

    Arguments
        R : the interest rate used to discount profits, in percent
        g : the growth rate of profits, in percent
    Returns
        the price-earnings ratio, P/E
    """
    # divide by 100 to turn the percentages into shares
    return 1 / ((R - g) / 100)
```

### Checking the key results

The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, using Islandia's baseline. First the 2008 story
of Fig. 2 with the IS/MP functions, and then the first year of the crisis in the AS/AD model.

```{python}
# Step 1: the cut that offsets the housing bust, and what firms pay once the crisis hits
R_ff = R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR
R = borrowing_rate(R_ff, F_CRISIS)

# Step 2: output at the three stages of Fig. 2. An f-string, f"... {value:.1f}",
# puts a value into the text; ":.1f" means "one decimal".
print(f"Housing bust, Fed does nothing (B):  Y~ = {is_output(R_BAR, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
print(f"Fed cuts R_ff to {R_ff:.1f}% (C):          Y~ = {is_output(R_ff, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
print(f"Risk premium f = 4, so R = {R:.1f}% (D):  Y~ = {is_output(R, A_HOUSING):.1f}%")
# equation (3): the fed funds rate that brings Y~ back to 0
print(f"Rate that restores Y~ = 0, eq. (3):  R_ff* = {R_BAR + A_HOUSING / B_BAR - F_CRISIS:.1f}%")

# Step 3: the AS/AD version. `Y, pi = solve_asad(...)` unpacks the two results
# of the function into two variables.
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS)
print(f"AS/AD, first year of the crisis:     Y~ = {Y:.1f}%, inflation = {pi:.1f}%")
```

The Fed's cut would fully offset the housing bust, but the risk premium undoes it and more: output ends 4 percent
below potential. In the AS/AD version the policy rule also reacts to inflation, so the first-year recession is
4 percent and inflation falls from 2 to 0 percent.

**Check 1: the crossing point lies on both curves, and the friction is a demand shock.** The output and inflation
from equation (5) must satisfy the AD curve (4) and the AS curve. And a premium $\bar{f}$ must do exactly what a
fall of $\bar{a}$ by $\bar{b}\bar{f}$ does.

```{python}
# Step 1: the crossing point from equation (5)
Y, pi = solve_asad(PI_BAR, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS)
print(f"Equation (5): Y~ = {Y:.3f}, pi = {pi:.3f}")
# Step 2: the point must lie on the AD curve (4) and on the AS curve
print(f"AD curve (4) at this pi:  Y~ = {ad_output(pi, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS):.3f}")
print(f"AS curve at this Y~:      pi = {as_inflation(Y):.3f}")
# Step 3: no premium, but a demand shock lower by b f: the same AD output
same = ad_output(pi, a=A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS, f=0.0)
print(f"AD with f = 4: {ad_output(pi, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS):.3f};  "
      f"AD with f = 0 and a lowered by b f: {same:.3f}")
```

**Check 2: the path of inflation.** We solve the AS/AD model year by year with equation (5) and compare inflation
with the closed form (7), which says the gap to $\pi_C$ shrinks by the factor $1/1.5$ each year.

```{python}
# Step 1: long-run inflation, equation (6), and the factor of equation (7)
pi_C = PI_BAR + (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS) / (B_BAR * M_BAR)     # equation (6)
factor = 1 / (1 + B_BAR * M_BAR * NU)
print(f"Long-run inflation, equation (6): pi_C = {pi_C:.2f}%")

# Step 2: solve year by year. `range(1, 9)` counts 1, 2, ..., 8, so the `for` loop
# runs its indented lines 8 times. `**` means "to the power of", and `{Y:6.2f}`
# shows two decimals in a space six characters wide, so that the columns line up.
pi_prev = PI_BAR                                  # inflation before the crisis
for t in range(1, 9):
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_prev, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS)
    closed = pi_C + factor ** t * (PI_BAR - pi_C)                      # equation (7)
    print(f"Year {t}: Y~ = {Y:6.2f}%   pi = {pi:6.3f}% (year by year)   {closed:6.3f}% (equation 7)")
    # `pi_prev = pi` hands this year's inflation on to the next year
    pi_prev = pi
```

**Check 3: the comparative statics.** We raise the premium by one point and compare the first-year effects and the
long-run inflation with the table: $-0.67$, $-0.33$ and $-1$.

```{python}
# Step 1: the first year with the baseline premium and with one point more
Y0, pi0 = solve_asad(PI_BAR, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS)
Y1, pi1 = solve_asad(PI_BAR, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS + 1)
# Step 2: long-run inflation, equation (6), in both cases
pi_C0 = PI_BAR + (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * F_CRISIS) / (B_BAR * M_BAR)
pi_C1 = PI_BAR + (A_HOUSING - B_BAR * (F_CRISIS + 1)) / (B_BAR * M_BAR)
# Step 3: the differences; ":+.3f" shows the sign and three decimals
print(f"One more point of f: first-year output {Y1 - Y0:+.3f}, first-year inflation {pi1 - pi0:+.3f}")
print(f"                     long-run inflation {pi_C1 - pi_C0:+.3f}")
```

**Check 4: the zero lower bound.** Equation (10) must give the same output as setting the nominal rate to zero and
going through the Fisher equation (8), equation (1) and the IS curve. Equation (9) shows when the rule hits the
bound.

```{python}
# A `for` loop can also run over a few values written in parentheses,
# here three inflation rates
for pi in (2.0, 0.0, -2.0):
    # Step 1: nominal rate zero, then the Fisher equation (8) and the premium (1)
    R_floor = borrowing_rate(real_rate(0.0, pi), F_CRISIS)
    direct = is_output(R_floor, A_HOUSING)
    # Step 2: compare with equation (10), and show the nominal rate rule (9) asks for
    print(f"pi = {pi:+.0f}%: best output {direct:+.1f}% (step by step), "
          f"{zlb_best_output(pi, A_HOUSING, F_CRISIS):+.1f}% (equation 10); "
          f"rule (9) asks for i = {R_BAR + pi + M_BAR * (pi - PI_BAR):+.1f}%")
```

**Check 5: the deflationary spiral.** We freeze the nominal rate at the 1929 level, $\bar{i} = \bar{r} + 3 = 5$
percent, start from the crash ($\bar{a}' = -3$, inflation zero) and let the real rate follow last year's inflation.
Equation (11) says each year's gap is 1.5 times the last.

```{python}
# Step 1: the nominal rate the Fed kept (inflation was about zero)
i_fixed = R_BAR + HIKE
pi_prev = 0.0
# year 1: the crash, point C
Y_prev = is_output(real_rate(i_fixed, pi_prev), A_CRASH)
print(f"Year 1: Y~ = {Y_prev:6.2f}%")

# Step 2: years 2 to 4, each with last year's inflation
for year in range(2, 5):
    # last year's slump lowered inflation ...
    pi_prev = as_inflation(Y_prev, pi_prev)
    # ... which raises this year's real rate
    Y = is_output(real_rate(i_fixed, pi_prev), A_CRASH)
    print(f"Year {year}: Y~ = {Y:6.2f}%   ratio to last year = {Y / Y_prev:.2f}  "
          f"(equation 11: {1 + B_BAR * NU:.2f})")
    Y_prev = Y
```

The first two years are the points $C$ and $D$ of Figs. 12 and 13, $-6$ and $-9$ percent.

**Check 6: leverage and asset prices.** We check equation (12) against a balance sheet written out in dollars,
and equation (13) against a long sum of discounted profits.

```{python}
# Step 1: a bank with a 7% capital ratio; its liabilities stay fixed in dollars
bank_assets, bank_capital = 100.0, 7.0
bank_debts = bank_assets - bank_capital
# the assets lose 3%
new_capital = bank_assets * (1 - 0.03) - bank_debts
print(f"Leverage = {bank_debts / bank_capital:.1f}; net worth {bank_capital:.0f} -> {new_capital:.0f}: "
      f"{100 * (new_capital / bank_capital - 1):.1f}% (balance sheet), "
      f"{net_worth_change(3, 0.07):.1f}% (equation 12)")

# Step 2: profits of 1 next year, growing 2% a year, discounted at 7%.
# `total += ...` is short for `total = total + ...`: it adds one more term each
# time the loop runs.
total = 0.0
for year in range(1, 2001):
    total += 1.02 ** (year - 1) / 1.07 ** year
print(f"P/E: {total:.2f} (sum of 2,000 years), {price_earnings(7, 2):.2f} (equation 13); "
      f"with R = 8%: {price_earnings(8, 2):.2f}, "
      f"a change of {100 * (price_earnings(8, 2) / price_earnings(7, 2) - 1):.0f}%")

# Step 3: forward guidance, equation (14): the long rate averages the short rates
print(f"Forward guidance, equation (14): {(0 + 1 + 2 + 3) / 4:.2f}% -> {(0 + 0 + 0 + 2) / 4:.2f}%")
```

### Drawing and data tools

The figures share a set of tools. The drawing tools put curves, points and arrows on the IS/MP and AS/AD
diagrams; the data tools shade the U.S. recessions, measure peaks and troughs, and give every country its own
color. Run them and move on, or open the box to see how they work.

<!-- cell -->

::: {.callout-note .mic-fold collapse="true" title="Show the drawing and data tools"}

All model diagrams use the same few drawing steps, so we write them once. `add_curve` draws one curve and writes
its name at its right end, and `add_label` leaves out a name that would sit on top of another one.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Drawing tools: curves and their names
# Step 1: faded colors for the curves before a shock
FADED_TEAL, FADED_BLUE = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)", "rgba(22,82,140,0.35)"


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of a panel.

    Arguments
        col : the panel, 1 or 2
    Returns
        the names of its axes: "x" and "y" in panel 1, "x2" and "y2" in panel 2
    """
    # Step 2: panel 1 has plain names, the others end in their number
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_label(fig, x, y, text, color, col=1):
    """Write a curve's name at (x, y), unless another name already sits close by.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to draw on
        x, y  : where the name goes, in axis units
        text  : the curve's name, e.g. "IS"
        color : its color, e.g. TEAL
        col   : the panel to write in
    """
    xref, yref = axis_names(col)
    # Step 3: a `for` loop over fig.layout.annotations looks at every name already
    # written; `abs` is the absolute value, and `return` inside the loop stops the
    # function early, so a name within 0.6 axis units is left out
    for old in fig.layout.annotations:
        if old.xref == xref and old.showarrow is False and abs(old.x - x) < 1.5 and abs(old.y - y) < 0.6:
            return
    # Step 4: no name close by: write this one
    fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=text, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                       yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, box, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw a curve in a panel and write its name at its last point inside the axes.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to draw on
        x, y  : the points of the curve (arrays)
        label : the curve's name ("" for none)
        color : its color
        box   : the axes, (x range, y range)
        dash  : "solid" or "dash"
        col   : the panel to draw in
    """
    # Step 1: draw the curve; `row=1, col=col` picks the panel. The arrays x and y
    # usually come from `np.linspace(-7.5, 4.5, 121)`, 121 evenly spaced numbers,
    # put through a model function, which works on a whole array at once
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    # Step 2: which points lie inside the axes? `&` is true where both conditions
    # hold, and the right edge leaves room for the text
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    inside = (x >= x0) & (x <= x1 - 1.2) & (y >= y0) & (y <= y1)
    # Step 3: `x[inside]` keeps the values where `inside` is true, and `[-1]`
    # takes the last of them: the name goes after the last point inside
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        add_label(fig, x[inside][-1], y[inside][-1], label, color, col)
```

`add_point` marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and `add_arrow` draws an arrow between two points.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Drawing tools: points and arrows
def add_point(fig, x, y, label, box, guides="v", col=1, where="top right"):
    """Mark (x, y) with a dot and a letter, with dashed guides to the axes.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        x, y   : the point, in axis units
        label  : its letter, e.g. "A"
        box    : the axes, (x range, y range)
        guides : "v" for a guide down to the x-axis, "both" for both axes, "none"
        col    : the panel to draw in
        where  : where the letter sits, e.g. "top right"
    """
    # Step 1: the dashed guides; by default one line, from the point down to the x-axis
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = box
    xs, ys = [x, x], [y, y0]
    # "both": from the y-axis across to the point, then down to the x-axis
    if guides == "both":
        xs, ys = [x0, x, x], [y, y, y0]
    # "none": no guides at all
    if guides != "none":
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=xs, y=ys, mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                                 line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=1, col=col)
    # Step 2: the dot and its letter
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[x], y=[y], mode="markers+text", text=[label], textposition=where,
                             name=label, showlegend=False, textfont=dict(size=16),
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units (none if the points almost coincide).

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        x0, y0 : where the arrow starts
        x1, y1 : where it points
        col    : the panel to draw in
    """
    # draw it only if the two points are visibly apart
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        # the arrow's tip (x, y) and tail (ax, ay), both in the panel's axis units
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")
```

`model_figure` starts a figure with one or two panels, and `model_axes` fixes the axes, so that you can see the
curves move, and writes the title.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Drawing tools: the panels and their fixed axes
def model_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with one or more panels side by side.

    Arguments
        cols   : the number of panels
        titles : one short title per panel (None for no titles)
    Returns
        the empty Plotly figure
    """
    # `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)` creates a figure with two panels side by side,
    # and `add_trace(..., row=1, col=2)` then draws in the second panel
    return make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)


def model_axes(fig, title, box, y_title, x_ticks, y_ticks, panels=1):
    """Fix the axes of every panel, so that you can see the curves move, and write the title.

    Arguments
        fig              : the figure
        title            : the title, with the readout of the sliders
        box              : the axes, (x range, y range)
        y_title          : the name of the vertical axis
        x_ticks, y_ticks : the tick values of the two axes
        panels           : the number of panels
    """
    # `fig.update_xaxes(..., row=1, col=col)` changes the horizontal axis of one
    # panel only, so the loop sets the axes panel by panel
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (%)", range=box[0], tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text=y_title, range=box[1], tickvals=y_ticks, zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title)
```

Two data tools are used by several figures. `shade_recessions` shades the U.S. recessions, as dated by the
National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). The file `recessions.csv` lists, for each recession since 1953, the
**peak** (the last month before the recession) and the **trough** (its last month). `peak_to_trough` finds the
highest value of a series between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall in percent between the two.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Data tools: recession shading and peak-to-trough falls
# Step 1: read the recession dates. `pd.read_csv` reads a data file into a
# DataFrame, a table with named columns, and `parse_dates=[...]` turns text
# such as "2007-12-01" into real dates.
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession, from peak to trough, that ends after the date start.

    Used in Figs. 4 and 6.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to draw on, with dates on the horizontal axis
        start : a date such as "1990-01-01"; recessions that end earlier are left out
    Returns
        the same figure, with the shading
    """
    # Step 2: `zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough)` hands over one (peak, trough)
    # pair at a time, and the `if` skips recessions that end before `start`
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    return fig


def peak_to_trough(data, column, start, end):
    """The peak of a series between two dates, the lowest value after it, and the fall.

    Used in Figs. 7 and 8.

    Arguments
        data       : a data table with a `date` column
        column     : the name of the series, e.g. "cape"
        start, end : the dates between which to look
    Returns
        three things: the peak row, the trough row and the fall in percent
    """
    # Step 3: keep the rows between the two dates; `&` requires both conditions
    window = data[(data.date >= start) & (data.date <= end)]
    # `.idxmax()` gives the row label of the largest value,
    # and `.loc[label]` picks that row
    peak = window.loc[window[column].idxmax()]
    # Step 4: the lowest value after the peak, and the fall from peak to trough
    after = window[window.date >= peak.date]
    trough = after.loc[after[column].idxmin()]
    return peak, trough, 100 * (1 - trough[column] / peak[column])


# Step 5: show the last three recessions of the file
recessions.tail(3)
```

**Beyond the United States.** The textbook's data figures are about the United States, but most of their series
exist for other countries too. Where they do, a subsection called *Beyond the United States* draws the same
series for many countries, with the textbook's countries picked to start with. Two more tools serve those charts:
`group_colors` gives every country a color that stays the same whichever countries you pick, and that no other
country shown with it uses, and `fit_axis` chooses the narrowest of a few fixed axis ranges that still holds every
point, so the axis only widens when a country needs it. The colors come from a palette of 44 colors.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Color tool: a palette of 44 colors
# Step 1: the colors that are too pale on a white page
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]
# Step 2: `px.colors.qualitative.Dark24` and `Alphabet` are lists of colors that
# Plotly ships with: 24 dark colors ...
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)
# ... and 20 more; `PALETTE.append(color)` adds a color at the end of the list
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
# Step 3: this blue is close to the U.S. navy: use it last
PALETTE.remove("#2E91E5")
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")
```

`group_colors` walks through the countries one by one and gives each the first color that no country shown with
it uses.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Color tool: one color for each country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries, in the order they get their colors
        groups : lists of countries shown together (the website menus)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the book's countries (None for none)
    Returns
        {country: color} for every country in names
    """
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        # a country with a fixed color keeps it; `continue` jumps to the next one
        if name in colors:
            continue
        # Step 1: the colors of the countries already shown with this one.
        # `colors.get(other)` is the color of `other`, or `None` if it has none yet.
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        # Step 2: free: not used in its groups; new: not used by any country
        free, new = [], []
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        # Step 3: `new + free + PALETTE` joins three lists and `[0]` takes the first
        # item: a color that no country uses yet if there is one, else one that no
        # country of the same groups uses
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors
```

`fit_axis` picks the first of a few fixed axis ranges that holds every value.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Drawing tool: an axis range that widens only when needed
def fit_axis(low, high, ranges):
    """The first range in the list that holds every value from low to high, else one that just fits.

    Arguments
        low, high : the lowest and highest values to show
        ranges    : a list of (bottom, top) ranges, narrowest first
    Returns
        the axis range [bottom, top]
    """
    # Step 1: `for bottom, top in ranges:` unpacks each pair of the list `ranges`
    for bottom, top in ranges:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    # Step 2: no range is wide enough: add 5% of room on each side
    pad = 0.05 * (high - low)
    return [low - pad, high + pad]
```

The website cannot run Python, so its versions of these charts draw every country at once and let you switch
them on in the legend. The next helper does that. Run it and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: folded
# @title Helper for the multi-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def legend_menu(fig, shown, groups=None):
    """Website version of a country picker: the countries in `shown` are drawn, the others wait in the legend.

    Without groups, every other country is in the legend ('legendonly'), one click away, and a menu offers
    "Show all". With groups, the menu puts one group at a time in the legend. Traces that are not countries
    (showlegend=False) always stay visible. The y-axis rescales to what is shown.

    Arguments
        fig    : a Plotly figure with one trace per country
        shown  : the countries drawn at the start
        groups : {menu label: [countries]}, or None for one "Show all" entry
    Returns
        the same figure, with the visibility set and the menu
    """
    def visibility(members):
        """Whether each trace is drawn, in the legend only, or hidden.

        Arguments
            members : the countries put in the legend (None for all)
        Returns
            one value per trace: True, "legendonly" or False
        """
        out = []
        for t in fig.data:
            # not a country, or a country shown at the start: drawn
            if t.showlegend is False or t.name in shown:
                out.append(True)
            # in the group: a click away
            elif members is None or t.name in members:
                out.append("legendonly")
            else:
                out.append(False)
        return out
    # Step 1: the menu entries, the textbook view first
    if groups is None:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility(None)}]),
                   dict(method="restyle", label="Show all", args=[{"visible": [True] * len(fig.data)}])]
    else:
        buttons = [dict(method="restyle", label="Textbook view", args=[{"visible": visibility([])}])]
        for label, members in groups.items():
            buttons.append(dict(method="restyle", label=label, args=[{"visible": visibility(members)}]))
    # Step 2: start with the textbook view, and make the website file smaller
    for trace, visible in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = visible
        compact(trace)
    # Step 3: let the y-axis rescale, and add the menu above the plot
    fig.layout.yaxis.range = None
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=0, direction="down", x=1, y=1.02,
                                        xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig


def compact(trace):
    """Shorter website files: dates without the time of day, values rounded to 2 decimals.

    Arguments
        trace : one curve of a Plotly figure, changed in place
    """
    # dates as plain text, e.g. "2008-09-01"
    if trace.x is not None and len(trace.x) > 0 and hasattr(trace.x[0], "strftime"):
        trace.x = pd.to_datetime(trace.x).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    # numbers with two decimals
    if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
        trace.y = np.round(np.asarray(trace.y), 2)


def region_groups(data):
    """The country groups of the website menus for long country lists, one per region.

    Arguments
        data : a data table with `country` and `region` columns
    Returns
        {"Add: " + region: [countries of the region, A to Z]}
    """
    groups = {}
    # one entry per region, with its countries sorted A to Z
    for region, rows in data.groupby("region"):
        groups["Add: " + region] = sorted(rows.country.unique())
    return groups
```

## Financial frictions in the short-run model

We first measure the financial friction in the data, then add it to the IS/MP and AS/AD diagrams to see why a crisis acts like a large negative demand shock.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: The spread between corporate bonds and 10-year Treasuries

**Goal.** See the financial friction $\bar{f}$ in the data: the gap between what companies and the government pay to
borrow.

The U.S. government almost surely repays its debt, so its 10-year bonds (*Treasuries*) are the safe benchmark. Companies
with a "BAA" rating are solid but not risk-free, so investors ask for a higher yield on their bonds. The difference
between the two yields, the **spread**, is a measure of the risk premium $\bar{f}$ in equation (1). In normal times
it is about 2 percentage points.

```{python}
# Load the data of Fig. 1: one row per month, the two yields and their spread
spread = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig14-1.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
spread.head()
```

Each row is a month. `baa_yield` and `treasury_10y` are the two yields in percent, and `spread` is their difference in
percentage points. Before plotting we give the columns readable names, because the names appear in the legend.

The cell below also finds the month with the largest spread, which the chart labels.

```{python}
# Step 1: readable names for the columns baa_yield, treasury_10y and spread;
# they appear in the legend
names = {
    "baa_yield": "BAA corporate bond yield",
    "treasury_10y": "10-year Treasury yield",
    "spread": "Spread",
}
# Step 2: the month with the largest spread. `.idxmax()` gives the row label of
# the largest value, and `.loc[label]` picks that row
peak = spread.loc[spread.spread.idxmax()]
```

```{python}

# Step 1: one line per column. `rename(columns=names)` gives the columns their
# readable names, and `list(names.values())` is the list of the new names.
# `px.line` draws a line chart from a DataFrame, one line per column of y
fig = px.line(
    spread.rename(columns=names),
    x="date",
    y=list(names.values()),
    color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, "#5aa0d8", BLUE],
    labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
    title="Corporate borrowing costs rose in 2008 while Treasury yields fell",
)
# Step 2: thin lines for the yields, a thick one for the spread;
# `selector=dict(name=...)` changes only the line with that name
fig.update_traces(line_width=2)
fig.update_traces(line_width=4, selector=dict(name="Spread"))
# an arrow and a label at the largest spread
fig.add_annotation(
    x=peak.date,
    y=peak.spread,
    text=f"Spread: {peak.spread:.1f} points ({peak.date:%b %Y})",
    ax=120,
    ay=-50,

)
# Step 3: fixed axes. `hovermode="x unified"` shows all three values of a month

fig.update_layout(
    yaxis=dict(range=[0, 10.5], tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
    hovermode="x unified",

    legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"),

fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Moody's, Seasoned Baa Corporate Bond Yield (`BAA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAA);
[Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Rate (`GS10`, H.15 release), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GS10).
The spread, BAA minus GS10, is our own calculation.
Prepared file: [`data/ch14/fig14-1.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch14/fig14-1.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch14/README.md)).

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- The spread averaged about 2 points from 1996 to 2007, then jumped to 6 points in December 2008, three times its usual
  size.
- In 2007–2008 the Treasury yield **fell**, as the Fed cut rates and investors fled to safety, but the BAA yield **rose**.
  Lower policy rates did not reach the companies that borrow.
- Smaller spikes come with other moments of stress: 2002, after the 2001 recession and the dot-com crash; the oil-price
  collapse of early 2016; and the Covid-19 shock of spring 2020.
